Metabolic and physiologic improvements from consuming a paleolithic, hunter-gatherer type diet

I have recently begun Paleo following a sports injury that has limited my ability to exercise. After some googling I found high protein intake and low carbohydrate intake mixed with glutamine supplements and whatever workouts I was able to do would be the best in helping preserve muscle in my time of being partially immobile.

Turns I love Paleo, and have had no issue dropping grains, sugars, and dairy products from my diet as I have seen these all as fillers and lacking flavor for the most part (except cheese but I still abstain).

I was on /r/paleo for a bit but reading through the posts I found that most of the people posting were barely Paleo as they still consumed sugars and dairy and were rather just on a basic low-carb diet. Hopefully this subverse will mature into something more worthwhile for people with a stronger resolve and interest in seeing long-term gains from being on an all nature hunter-gatherer regiment.

Good morning, this coming Sunday a buddy and myself are going to attempt smoking some pork shoulder. We are both new to smoking and I'd like to get some tips. I've watched videos on YouTube and gone to various websites but wanted to see what voat has to offer in terms of insight or tips. I don't have a picture of his rig and from what he told there is no smoke box. Thanks and please be gentle!
New to smoking looking for advice.

If I were you, I would use a boston butt over a pork shoulder, more meat and less bones. I just posted this in another thread so here you go:

Pork butts are actually really easy and very forgiving. Start early in the day, wrap in foil at 150 degrees and pull at 195-200, let it rest and then shred. Make sure to keep the juice from the wrap to pour over the pork. Serve with a mustard/vinegar sauce.

Make sure you use a rub with a good amount of brown sugar. Try and get pecan wood for the smoke.
Thanks! I'll talk to my buddy see if he hasn't already purchased the meat.

Smoking is all about indirect heat - keep your meat as far away from the fire as you can. Google 'minion method' for keeping a low and slow temp for a long cook.

If charcoal is your main fuel source, add wood chips or chunks for that smokey flavor. Don't soak the wood chips.

Smoking is about a balance between moisture retention and getting the meat hot enough so that the connective tissue turns to sweet, sweet gelatin. Too hot too fast and you get tough, dry meat.

Cook to temperature, not to time. It's ready when it's ready.

I usually wrap in foil around 155 degrees. Meats have a tendency to stall around that temp (stay at the same temp for a long time) - wrapping in foil helps get over that hump, and retain moisture.

Pork butt is done for me at 202-204 degrees. Then I let it rest for awhile still in the foil. I think this helps the moisture move back into the center of the butt.

Put a drip pan under the meat to catch drippings. I like to pour those drippings through a fat separator and use the juice as a sauce. Good stuff!
Thanks for tips! Hoping to put them to good use.

If charcoal is your main fuel source, add wood chips or chunks for that smokey flavor. Don't soak the wood chips.

Why wouldn't you want to soak the wood chips/chunks? Too much smoke? I've always soaked my wood, but I usually make brisket and like the very smokey flavor.

Soaking the chips just creates steam. The water doesn't penetrate the wood.

http://amazingribs.com/tips_and_technique/mythbusting_soaking_wood.html
Thanks for the information and especially the link. Very informational!

I use a pellet smoker and do my shoulders at 250 until they reach 200-205. Beware the stall at ~150. You can wrap, I don't. The wrap will power through the stall, but I find it softens the bark. Your choice; either way it will get through the stall. If you're doing one big piece of meat you can cut it in half for more bark and a somewhat quicker cook time. But always cook to temp never time. You'll see / hear lots of x hours per pound advice. These should always be considered guessimations. So many variables can affect cook time so go with the internal temp and you'll not go wrong. Good luck and happy smokes. It's a great way to cook meats.
Thanks! I am definitely hearing a lot of cook to temp and not time so I'll make sure I follow that.
